ITM (EPSG:2157) is the current standard for Irish spatial data — GPS points enter Irish workflows through it.
Irish planning and heritage records cite grid references habitually. Converting correctly is the difference between the right field and the next county.
The island has one geography and two grid traditions (plus the UK's). All-island work needs the distinctions this page exists to explain.

Same point, two coordinate pairs: the older Irish Grid (EPSG:29903) and ITM differ by up to a couple of hundred metres in places — enough to matter, small enough to be confused silently. The systems must be named, not assumed.
Irish Grid references pair a lettered 100 km square (A–Z, skipping I) with digits inside it — Dublin's square is O. The pattern mirrors Britain's, with Ireland's own origins and letters.

faq: What is the difference between ITM and the older Irish Grid?

Different datums, projections and origins: ITM (Irish Transverse Mercator, EPSG:2157) is the modern ETRS89-based system; the Irish Grid (EPSG:29903) rides the Ireland 1975 datum. Coordinates for the same point differ — noticeably at field scale. This helper exists to keep the two from being silently mixed.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84, the frame web maps and GPS share — tile and pixel systems on this page are defined over it.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
No — pixels and tiles quantise the world; extra coordinate decimals beyond the cell size are decoration.
Can I copy the result into GIS software?
Yes — set the layer CRS correctly (2157 for ITM, 29903 for Irish Grid) or the software will faithfully plot your point in the wrong county.
Northern Ireland?
Both systems cover the whole island — grid geography ignores the border even where administration does not. UK national mapping additionally uses the British grid for some purposes.
The letter I is missing — typo?
Deliberate: I is skipped in the letter squares to avoid confusion with 1, the same courtesy as the British grid.
Townland references?
Ireland's townlands predate grids; references in heritage records pair townland names with grid references. The grid part converts here; the names are their own scholarship.
Precision of digits?
As with all grid references: digit pairs set the grain — 4 figures = 1 km, 6 = 100 m, 8 = 10 m, 10 = 1 m.
Sea points?
The grids project over coastal waters; references remain a land habit, and offshore work speaks lat/lon.
Which should new work use?
ITM — the current national standard. The old grid is for reading the archive, which is half of Irish fieldwork.
